passage: On the verandah of their village house, two-year-old Tenzin sat with his rubber chappals. His mother Nirmala bent to help. "No! Me do!" He pushed her hand away and jammed a foot in, the wrong one. He tried again, frowning, tongue out. Nirmala sat back and waited. At last both were on, back to front. He stamped proudly. Then a dog barked at the gate, and Tenzin ran straight into her lap and held on tight.

qa.q: What did Tenzin say when Nirmala bent to help?
qa.a: "No! Me do!"

qa.q: What does Tenzin running into Nirmala's lap after the dog barked show?
qa.a: He still needs her for safety when scared, only minutes after insisting on doing things himself.

qa.q: Which of Nirmala's choices helped Tenzin feel capable?
qa.a: She sat back and waited instead of taking over, even though the chappals ended up back to front.

qa.q: What might it be like for Nirmala to be pushed away and then clung to?
qa.a: It may feel funny and tender at once, seeing her son want both independence and her closeness 🙂

grounding: A toddler insists on putting on his own chappals, then runs to his mother for safety minutes later.

passage: At the door of their flat in Toronto, Esther held out Abebe's snowsuit. "Arms in, sweetheart." "Me!" Abebe, not quite three, grabbed the zip and tugged. It stuck. He tugged harder and roared. Esther's hand hovered. Then she held the bottom of the zip steady and let him pull. Up it went. "I did it!" He marched to the door alone. Outside, the wind hit his face, and he turned and lifted both arms. "Mama, carry."

qa.q: What did Abebe try to do himself?
qa.a: Pull up the zip of his snowsuit.

qa.q: Why did Abebe roar when the zip stuck?
qa.a: He was frustrated because he badly wanted to do it himself and the zip wouldn't move.

qa.q: What was clever about how Esther helped with the zip?
qa.a: She held the bottom steady but let Abebe pull, so he still got to do it himself.

qa.q: How might Esther feel when Abebe says "Mama, carry" right after marching off alone?
qa.a: She may smile at how fast he swings between independence and needing her, and be glad to hold him.

grounding: A toddler insists on zipping his own snowsuit, then asks to be carried as soon as the cold wind hits.

passage: I'm Varun, Nitin's uncle. On Sunday my sister tried to put on his sandals, and two-year-old Nitin yelled, "Nitin do it!" and pushed her hand away. He struggled with the strap for ages. Nobody was allowed to touch. When one was done, he looked at me as if he had won a match. Then the pressure cooker whistled, and he ran and grabbed his mother's leg and wouldn't let go.

qa.q: What did Nitin yell when his mother tried to help?
qa.a: "Nitin do it!"

qa.q: What does Nitin's look after finishing one sandal suggest?
qa.a: He felt proud and triumphant, as if he had won a match.

qa.q: How could Nitin's mother respond when he grabs her leg after the whistle?
qa.a: She can hold him and reassure him, then let him go back to the sandals when he's ready.

qa.q: How might Varun see Nitin's switch from "Nitin do it!" to clinging?
qa.a: As an uncle watching, he sees both needs one after the other: wanting to do it alone and wanting his mother close.

grounding: An uncle watches a toddler insist on doing his sandals alone and then cling to his mother minutes later.

passage:
Monday. Preeti, two, climbed the step stool at the basin. Her mother, Jahnavi, reached for the tap. "No! Me do!" Preeti pushed the hand away and splashed water everywhere.
Wednesday. Preeti soaped her own hands, very slowly. Then a crow cawed at the window. She dropped the soap and scrambled into Jahnavi's arms, face hidden.
Friday. "Me do," she said again, and did. Then she held up her dripping hands for Jahnavi to dry, and leaned against her knees.

qa.q: What did Preeti climb at the basin?
qa.a: She climbed the step stool.

qa.q: Why did Preeti scramble into Jahnavi's arms on Wednesday?
qa.a: The crow's caw startled her, and even while wanting to do things herself, she needed her mother to feel safe.

qa.q: What could Jahnavi keep doing to support both sides of Preeti?
qa.a: Let Preeti try things herself while staying close enough to hold her when she gets scared.

qa.q: What might Jahnavi feel on Friday when Preeti washes alone and then leans against her?
qa.a: She may feel proud of Preeti's new skill and warm that Preeti still wants her close.

grounding: Over a week a two-year-old insists on washing her hands herself yet runs to her mother for safety, showing independence and need together.

passage:
The monsoon had flooded the lane below their Dadar flat, and Lavanya, two, had new yellow gumboots. When her mother, Hansa, knelt to help, Lavanya shoved her hand away. "Me do it!" She sat on the floor, pulled and grunted, and got one boot on the wrong foot. Hansa waited. The second went on right. Lavanya stamped proudly to the door.
In the lift, a big dog barked on the second floor. Lavanya dropped her umbrella and clung to Hansa's leg with both arms until the doors closed.

qa.q: What colour were Lavanya's new gumboots?
qa.a: They were yellow.

qa.q: How did Lavanya feel as she stamped to the door?
qa.a: She felt proud that she had put the boots on herself.

qa.q: What did Hansa do well while Lavanya struggled with the boots?
qa.a: She waited instead of taking over, so Lavanya could manage alone, and was still there to cling to in the lift.

qa.q: How might Hansa feel when Lavanya clings to her leg minutes after refusing help?
qa.a: She might feel tender and a little amused, seeing that Lavanya needs both independence and her safety. 🙂

grounding: A toddler refuses help with her boots, then clings to her mother minutes later when a dog barks, showing independence and need for safety together.
